newsitem.title: FRANCE: Tunisia says wheat, barley needs well covered.
newsitem.headline: Tunisia says wheat, barley needs well covered.

text.p: Tunisia may stay out of the grain market for a while, having covered its wheat import needs until end-September and its barley requirements until November, a Tunisian cereals authority official said on Tuesday.
"We recently bought (wheat) for up until end-September...We can easily wait," procurement director Assia Bejaoui told Reuters by telephone from Tunis.
"Regarding barley we are covered until November, so there are no new purchases in the pipeline," she added.
But Tunisia would react promptly if world prices fell sharply.
"We will not be buyers on the world market soon. But if there was a spectacular fall (in prices), of course we would be there to take advantage of it," she said.
Bejaoui confirmed that in late June Tunisia bought 150,000 tonnes of U.S. wheat. Grain traders priced the purchase at $148.21 and $159.95 per tonne, cost and freight, for August-October shipment.
In April Tunisia bought 100,000 tonnes of optional-origin feed barley for shipment between September and November at $136.72, including cost and freight, exporters said.
The latest Tunisian wheat deal was part of a series of North African purchases prompted by a decline in world prices because of strong harvest progress in the U.S.
Bejaoui said Tunisia was in a comfortable position, having bought when world prices were low.
She said the trend for world wheat prices was bearish, but operators would have a clearer picture in the autumn of how crops, particularly in the European Union, were shaping up.
She said there were fears that rains in June might hit the quality of European wheat. "It rained in Europe, so this can lead to wheat germination and cut quality."
Another key element in the outlook for world prices would be the timing of the return of the EU to world markets, she said.
Last week the EU agreed to open grain export tenders for the new 1997/98 campaign but has said it was in no hurry to start shipping its grain amid conflicting reports on the new crop.
Bejaoui said she expected te EU to take a decision in September.
"We will see in September if the EU decides to grant export subsidies and if prices continue to decline."
She said prospects for the Tunisian grain harvest were very average, but she did not provide any figures.
Tunisia's wheat consumption would remain steady this year at some 75,000 tonnes per month.
The London-based International Grains Council said last month that dry conditions would sharply cut wheat producton in Tunisia, which might double wheat imports to 1.2 million tonnes in 1997/98.
